Pechenegs: Extinct Turkic people. The Pechenegs or Patzinaks, were a semi-nomadic Turkic people from Central Asia who spoke the Pecheneg language.
Serving as the 64th Bishop of Rome from 590 until 604, this former Roman prefect sent missionaries to England, including Augustine of Canterbury — who was he?
Pope Gregory I: 64th Bishop of Rome; head of the Roman Catholic Church from AD 590 to 604.
In October 2021, this U.S. assistant secretary for health became the nation's first openly transgender four-star officer across all eight uniformed services — who is she?
Rachel Levine: American public health official (born 1957)

This short-lived 1990s state in the Balkans seceded from a disintegrating Yugoslavia in 1992, triggering a three-year war as rival Serb and Croat factions carved out their own unrecognized quasi-states — what state?
Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Balkan country (1992–1995)

A vocal critic of the Federal Reserve and mass surveillance programs, this Texas congressman ran for president as the Libertarian nominee in 1988 before seeking the Republican nomination twice more — who is he?

In 1982 this child from Manchester, Maine wrote a letter to Soviet leader Yuri Andropov — and got a personal reply inviting her to visit the USSR, making her 'America's Youngest Ambassador' — who was she?
Samantha Smith: American child peace activist (1972–1985)
Once a commander of Alexander the Great's elite infantry, this Macedonian general later ruled Asia Minor, Syria, Mesopotamia, and Iran, founding an empire that bore his name — who was he?
Seleucus I Nicator: Macedonian general, Diadochus, and founder of the Seleucid Empire.
Spanning Emperor Hirohito's reign from 1926 to 1989, this period saw Japan's wartime totalitarian turn, defeat in World War II, and a nearly seven-year American-led occupation — which era?
Shōwa era: Period of Japanese history (1926–1989)
Based on the island of Sumatra, this maritime empire became a key center for spreading Buddhism across Southeast Asia between the 7th and 11th centuries — which empire?
Srivijaya: Empire based on Sumatra (c. 671–1025 AD)
A military engineer who is a national hero in Poland, Lithuania, Belarus AND the United States, he fought for the American Revolution before leading an uprising in 1794 — who was he?
This centrist political position blends economically liberal ideas with social democratic policy, favoring workfare over welfare — what's it called?
Third Way: Centrist political position. The Third Way has been promoted by social liberal and social-democratic parties.
A law professor with a doctorate from the London School of Economics, she became the first woman to serve as president of the Republic of China, from 2016 to 2024 — who is she?

Tsai Ing-wen: President of the Republic of China from 2016 to 2024. Following the DPP's defeat in the 2008 presidential election, Tsai was elected party chair, a position she held three times (2008–2012, 2014–2018, and 2020–2022).

This King of Italy also claimed the titles Emperor of Ethiopia and King of the Albanians after Italy's invasions of those countries, and reigned through the entire rise and fall of the Fascist regime — who was he?
Victor Emmanuel III: King of Italy from 1900 to 1946.
Nicknamed the "Land Cruiser War," this conflict erupted in Sudan in 2003 and led to President Omar al-Bashir being indicted for genocide by the International Criminal Court. What was it?
War in Darfur: Genocidal conflict in Western Sudan.
Also known as the Prince of Orange, he led the Dutch revolt against Spanish Habsburg rule that ignited the Eighty Years' War and eventually won the United Provinces their independence — who is he?
William the Silent: Dutch revolt leader (1533–1584)

Born to a family of strawberry farmers in Akita Prefecture, this politician rose to become Japan's Prime Minister from 2020 to 2021 after years as Chief Cabinet Secretary under Shinzo Abe — who is he?

Yoshihide Suga: Prime Minister of Japan from 2020 to 2021. Yoshihide Suga (菅 義偉, Suga Yoshihide; born 6 December 1948) is a Japanese former politician who served as Prime Minister of Japan from 2020 to 2021.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
Who among these four was born earliest?
George Grove (born 1820) is the earliest of the four. Grove was trained as a civil engineer, and successful in that profession, but his love of music drew him into musical administration.
Which of these four began earliest?
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the astronomer from these four.
Fritz Zwicky is an astronomer. Fritz Zwicky (German: [ˈtsvɪki]; February 14, 1898 – February 8, 1974) was a Swiss astronomer.
Which of these four is a mathematician?
What is the atomic number of Ruthenium?
Ruthenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ru and atomic number 44.
What is the atomic number of Chlorine?
Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
In what year was Ernest Lawrence born?
Ernest Lawrence: A graduate of the University of South Dakota and University of Minnesota, Lawrence obtained a PhD in physics at Yale in 1925.
In what year was Richard Feynman born?
Richard Feynman: Richard Phillips Feynman (May 11, 1918 – February 15, 1988) was an American theoretical physicist.
In what year was Klaus Schwab born?
Klaus Schwab: Klaus Martin Schwab (German: [klaʊs ˈmaʁtiːn ʃvaːp]; born 30 March 1938) is a German mechanical engineer, economist, and founder of the World Economic Forum (WEF).
In what year did Saint Valentine die?
Saint Valentine was a clergyman – either a priest or a bishop – in the Roman Empire who ministered to persecuted Christians.
In what year did Niels Bohr die?
Niels Bohr: Although the Bohr model has been supplanted by other models, its underlying principles remain valid.
In what year was Benzene discovered?
Benzene is an organic chemical compound with the molecular formula C6H6.
Perl: Larry Wall. Perl is a high-level, general-purpose, interpreted, dynamic programming language.
IAI Kfir: Israel Aerospace Industries Ltd.
Which country is Beriev A-50 from?
Beriev A-50: Russia. Developed to replace the Tupolev Tu-126 "Moss", the A-50 first flew in 1978.
Who is credited with discovering Penicillin?
Penicillin: Alexander Fleming. Penicillin was discovered in 1928 by the Scottish physician Alexander Fleming as a crude extract of P. rubens.
2C-B: Alexander Shulgin. 2C-B, also known as 4-bromo-2,5-dimethoxyphenethylamine or by names such as Nexus or Erox, is a psychedelic drug of the phenethylamine and 2C families.
Who is credited with discovering Chromium?
Chromium: Louis Nicolas Vauquelin. Chromium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cr and atomic number 24.
When a message is designed to spark an immediate purchase, it's called the 'direct-response' kind of this consumer-facing practice. What is it?
Advertising is the practice and techniques employed to bring attention to a product or service.
Its type species, a common freshwater organism constantly studied in classrooms and labs, lends its name to an entire genus of shape-changing single-celled organisms — what's the genus?
Amoeba (genus) is a genus of single-celled amoeboids in the family Amoebidae.

This superfamily of tailless Old World primates, native to sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia and more closely related to Old World monkeys than New World ones, includes humans among its members — what's this group called?
Ape (hominoids), are a superfamily of Old World simians native to sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia.
These large Old World monkeys come in six distinct species, each native to a different region of Africa, with one species also found on the Arabian Peninsula — what primate is it?
Baboon are primates comprising the genus Papio, one of the 23 genera of Old World monkeys, in the family Cercopithecidae.
From molecules and cells up to whole ecosystems, this science studies living things through ideas like heredity, evolution, and homeostasis — what is it?
Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms.
This rhythmic bodily process draws oxygen-rich air into the lungs and expels carbon dioxide, powering the cellular chemistry that turns food into energy — what process is it?
Breathing (respiring or ventilating) is the rhythmic process of inhaling air into the lungs providing oxygen, and exhaling the air removing carbon dioxide, in the gas exchange process.
Indigenous to Asia, this genus of flowering plants includes species like sativa, indica, and ruderalis, and is also commonly known as hemp when grown for non-drug purposes — name the genus?
Cannabis is a genus of flowering plants in the family Cannabaceae that is widely accepted as being indigenous to and originating from the continent of Asia.

The only living member of its genus, this big cat sprints at up to 104 km/h thanks to powerful hindlimbs, long legs, and a flexible spine, and wears black tear-like streaks down its face; which animal is it?
Cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) is a species of large feline and the only living member of the genus Acinonyx.
Mostly belonging to the genus Naja, these venomous snakes are known for rearing upward and flaring a distinctive hood when threatened — name this common snake type?
Cobra is the common name of various venomous snakes, most of which belong to the genus Naja.
Tolerant of poor, sandy soil, this legume was domesticated in Africa millennia ago and is now grown far more in Nigeria and Niger than anywhere else on Earth — which crop?
Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) is an annual herbaceous legume from the genus Vigna.

First patented in Germany in 1920, then independently synthesized by an American chemist in 1932 and marketed in German-speaking Europe as Permonid for its fast onset and short duration, what is this semi-synthetic opioid?
Desomorphine (or in some formulations known as Krokodil) is a semi-synthetic opioid commercialized by Roche, with powerful, fast-acting effects, such as sedation and analgesia.
This soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida is also known by slang names like 'dew-worm,' 'rainworm,' and 'nightcrawler.' What creature is it?
Earthworm is a soil-dwelling terrestrial invertebrate that belongs to the phylum Annelida.
Comprising around 50 species mostly found in the tropics, this fungal genus infects rye, wheat, barley, and other grasses, producing toxic alkaloids — name the group of fungi?
Ergot is a group of fungi of the genus Claviceps. The most prominent member of this group is Claviceps purpurea (rye ergot fungus).
The excessive buildup of collagen-rich connective tissue after chronic inflammation or repeated injury, leaving a permanent scar that can choke off organ function — what's this process called?
Fibrosis is the development of fibrous connective tissue in response to an injury.

This computer scientist demonstrated a working prototype of his operating system CP/M in 1974 and later founded Digital Research — his invention of the BIOS helped make the personal computer revolution possible. Who is he?
Gary Kildall (May 19, 1942 - July 11, 1994) was an American computer scientist and microcomputer entrepreneur.

Five species of this group of plants — rice, wheat, maize, barley, and sugar cane — together cover 46 percent of the world's arable land, alongside two related families, sedges and rushes. What kind of plant is this?
Grass refers to various families of plants.
Which 19th-century American economist's wildly popular treatise Progress and Poverty argued that a single tax on the value of land could build a more just and productive society?
Henry George (September 2, 1839 - October 29, 1897) was an American political economist, social philosopher and journalist.
A body-temperature emergency defined as a reading above 104°F, this condition kills roughly half a million people annually and is most commonly triggered by heat stroke — what is it called?
Hyperthermia is a condition in which an individual's body temperature is elevated beyond normal due to failed thermoregulation.
This medical condition describes a restricted blood supply to tissue or an organ, starving cells of the oxygen they need and often resulting from a blocked or narrowed vessel — what is it called?
Ischemia is a restriction in blood supply to any tissue, muscle group, or organ of the body.
This Confederate veteran and pharmacist sold the rights to his 1886 beverage recipe to Asa Griggs Candler for about $2,300 shortly before he died — who is he?
John Stith Pemberton (July 8, 1831 - August 16, 1888) was an American pharmacist, chemist, and Confederate States Army officer who is best known as the inventor of Coca-Cola.
Endemic to New Zealand, this large, nocturnal, ground-dwelling parrot has owl-like forward-facing eyes and holds the title of the world's only flightless parrot — what bird is it?
Kākāpō (Mori:; pl.: kkp; Strigops habroptilus), sometimes known as the owl-parrot, is a species of large, nocturnal, ground-dwelling parrot of the superfamily Strigopoidea.
Popular in aquariums but a destructive invader in the Atlantic and Mediterranean, this venomous Indo-Pacific creature warns predators off with bold red and black stripes — what is it?
Lionfish (genus Pterois) are venomous marine fish native to the Indo-Pacific.
Domesticated in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago from wild teosinte, this grain was grown by Native Americans alongside beans and squash in the 'Three Sisters' method — name the tall grass crop?
Maize (Zea mays), also known as corn, is a tall stout grass that produces cereal grain.
Driven by hormones, this coordinated pair of bodily rhythms — one governing the ovaries, the other the uterine lining — usually runs 21 to 35 days and begins around age 12. What is it called?
Menstrual cycle is a series of natural changes in hormone production and the structures of the uterus and ovaries of the female reproductive system that makes pregnancy possible.
Named from a Greek word for lead because its ores were once confused with lead ore, this chemical element bears the symbol Mo and atomic number 42 — name the element?
Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.

What term, coined in the mid-19th century and often attributed to pathologist Rudolf Virchow, describes the premature death of cells in living tissue due to external injury or infection, as opposed to programmed cell death?
Necrosis (from Ancient Greek (nkrsis) 'death') is a form of cell injury which results in the premature death of cells in living tissue by autolysis.

Synthesized in 2002 at a lab near Moscow and named in 2016 for the physicist who hunted down the heaviest atoms, this synthetic element claims the highest atomic number and atomic mass of anything yet known — which is it?
Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
Usually numbering four and tucked behind the thyroid, these small endocrine structures release a hormone that kicks in when blood calcium runs low — which structures?
Parathyroid gland are small endocrine glands in the neck of humans and other tetrapods.
This herbaceous annual vine produces edible pods and comes in bush or climbing cultivars; global output hit 28 million tonnes in 2022, led by India. What legume species is it?
Phaseolus vulgaris is a herbaceous annual plant. Its botanical classification, along with other Phaseolus species, is as a member of the legume family, Fabaceae.

This medical condition occurs when air collects in the space between the lung and chest wall, typically causing sudden, sharp one-sided chest pain and shortness of breath — what's the condition called?
Pneumothorax is collection of air in the pleural space between the lung and the chest wall.
Originating in Central Asia despite widespread cultivation elsewhere, this is the most commonly grown species of a fuzzy-skinned stone fruit — what is its scientific name?
Prunus armeniaca is the most commonly cultivated apricot species.
The only member of the genus Rangifer, this circumpolar deer of the Arctic tundra goes by another name entirely in North America — what is it?
Reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) is a species of deer with circumpolar distribution, native to Arctic, subarctic, tundra, boreal, and mountainous regions of Northern Europe, Siberia, and North America.
A botanist active in Japan's Meiji era, this scholar died in 1899 after decades of scientific work — who was he?
Ryōkichi Yatabe (October 13, 1851 - August 8, 1899) was a Japanese botanist during the Meiji era.
This veteran of six spaceflights was the first Russian cosmonaut to fly aboard NASA's Space Shuttle, on mission STS-60 — who is he?
Sergei Krikalev (born 27 August 1958) is a Russian mechanical engineer and former cosmonaut.

Barred from a formal education, she learned mathematics from her father's library and wrote to Gauss under the male pseudonym 'Monsieur Le Blanc,' later winning a Paris Academy prize for her work on elasticity. Which French mathematician was she?
Sophie Germain (1 April 1776 - 27 June 1831) was a French mathematician, physicist, and philosopher.
This towering perennial grass, native to New Guinea, stores so much natural sweetness in its jointed stalks that it's the world's primary source for a common sweetener — what plant is it?
Sugarcane is a species of tall, perennial grass (in the genus Saccharum, tribe Andropogoneae) that is used for sugar production.

Named for the order of fish that includes pufferfish, this potent neurotoxin also turns up in blue-ringed octopuses and rough-skinned newts, and is actually produced by symbiotic bacteria rather than the animals themselves — what's the toxin?

Tetrodotoxin (TTX) is a potent neurotoxin. Its name derives from Tetraodontiformes, an order that includes pufferfish, porcupinefish, ocean sunfish, and triggerfish; several of these species carry the toxin.

A phenylpiperazine compound in the serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor class, this antidepressant treats depression, anxiety and insomnia but carries a rare risk of prolonged, painful erections — which drug?
Trazodone is an antidepressant medication used to treat major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, and insomnia.
Mammals, birds, amphibians, fish, and reptiles all belong to this subphylum of animals, united by a backbone and a braincase — what is it?
Vertebrate are animals with a vertebral column and a cranium.
Though classified as a woodwind, this conical-bodied instrument is usually made of brass and uses a vibrating single reed to produce sound. What instrument is it?
Xoloitzcuintle (or Xoloitzquintle, Xoloitzcuintli, or Xolo) is one of several breeds of hairless dog.
Named for the skull-shaped marking on its thorax and first classified by Carl Linnaeus in 1758, this large moth was immortalized on the poster for 'The Silence of the Lambs' — which insect?
Acherontia atropos: Species of moth. It is most commonly identified by the vaguely skull-shaped pattern adorning the thorax, the characteristic from which its common and scientific names are derived.
Scientifically named Gadus chalcogrammus, this schooling member of the cod family gathers in massive numbers in the eastern Bering Sea — which fish?
Alaska pollock: Species of fish. The Alaska pollock also known as Pacific pollock or walleye pollock (Gadus chalcogrammus) is a marine fish species of the cod genus Gadus and family Gadidae.
Nicknamed 'whip-spiders' or 'tailless whip-scorpions,' these arachnids have no silk, no venom, and a name meaning 'blunt tail' — they grab with their pedipalps instead of biting — what order is this?
Amblypygi: Order of arachnids. The name "amblypygid" means "blunt tail", a reference to a lack of the flagellum that is otherwise seen in whip-scorpions.
Brought to Asia by Spanish traders aboard the Manila galleons, this tropical American tree produces a knobby, sweet fruit known as sugar apple or custard apple — what is this plant?
Annona squamosa: Species of tree. Annona squamosa is a small, well-branched tree or shrub from the family Annonaceae that bears edible fruits called sugar apples or sweetsops or custard apples.
This pigmented ring of skin around the nipple contains sebaceous glands as well as the openings of the milk ducts — what's it called?
Areola: Pigmented area on the breast around the nipple.
This genus of early African hominins, which lived during the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene, is considered ancestral to the genus that includes modern humans — which genus?
Australopithecus: Genus of hominin ancestral to modern humans. The genera Homo (which includes modern humans), Paranthropus, and Kenyanthropus evolved from some Australopithecus species.
With more than 2,000 species and petals but no sepals, this flowering plant genus originated in Africa and is popular as an ornamental houseplant in cooler climates — which genus?
Begonia: Genus of perennial flowering plants.

Despite its name, this African animal's hide actually ranges from brown to grey, and it's distinguished from its 'white' cousin by a pointed, hooked upper lip rather than a wide, square one — which species?
Black rhinoceros: Species of mammal. Although the species is referred to as black, its colours vary from brown to grey.
Named for its unusually long forelimbs — Greek for 'arm lizard' — this Late Jurassic sauropod was first described in 1903 from fossils found in Colorado — which dinosaur?
Brachiosaurus: Sauropod dinosaur genus from the late Jurassic Period.
Caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, this disease triggered a global health emergency declared by the WHO in March 2020 and lifted in May 2023 — which disease?
COVID-19: Contagious disease caused by SARS-CoV-2. Starting in January 2020, the disease spread worldwide, resulting in the COVID-19 pandemic.

This group of heart-muscle diseases includes the 'broken heart syndrome' type and can lead to irregular heartbeats, fainting, or even sudden cardiac death — what's the general term for this condition?
Cardiomyopathy: Disease of the heart muscle. In dilated cardiomyopathy the ventricles enlarge and weaken.
Also known as an ischemic stroke, this necrotic brain condition is the second-leading cause of death worldwide and a leading cause of physical disability — what is it?
Cerebral infarction: Stroke resulting from lack of blood flow.
Every animal in this group shares five telltale traits — including a notochord, pharyngeal slits, and a tail that extends past the anus — at some stage of life; which of these belongs to that phylum?
Chordate: Phylum of animals having a dorsal nerve cord.
Also nicknamed the 'Maybug' or 'doodlebug,' this European scarab beetle's males swarm during mating season while females stay put munching leaves that release telltale scent chemicals — which beetle?
Cockchafer: Species of scarab beetle. The cockchafer develops via metamorphosis, in which the beetle undergoes stages of eggs, larvae, pupae and adults.
These colonial marine invertebrates secrete calcium carbonate to build the hard skeletons that form tropical reefs — what are they?
Coral: Marine invertebrates of the subphylum Anthozoa.
Named for the ancient Greek word for a ship's helmsman, this transdisciplinary field studies feedback loops and circular causal processes across engineering, biology, and social systems — what is it?

Cybernetics: Study of circular causal processes. Cybernetics' transdisciplinary character means that it intersects with a number of other fields, resulting in a wide influence and diverse interpretations.
This medical and surgical specialty treats everything from inflammatory conditions and cancers to hair loss, requiring about four years of training beyond medical school — what field is it?
Dermatology: Field of medicine dealing with the hair, nails, skin, and its diseases.
Developed from the civilian DC-3 airliner and nicknamed 'Dakota' by the RAF, which WWII transport plane hauled troops, cargo, and paratroopers for roughly 100 countries' militaries?
Douglas C-47 Skytrain: Military transport aircraft derived from DC-3.

Defined by permanently erect fangs at the front of the mouth and ranging from a 7-inch white-lipped snake to a nearly 19-foot king, which snake family includes most of the world's neck-flaring venomous serpents?
Elapidae: Family of venomous snakes. The family includes 55 genera with around 360 species and over 170 subspecies.

This Irish experimental physicist shared the 1951 Nobel with John Cockcroft for splitting the atom — the first nuclear transmutation, as the prize committee put it, "entirely under human control." Who was he?
Introduced to North America as early as 1840, this large eusocial wasp builds paper-like nests and preys on beetles, other wasps, and dragonflies — which insect is it?
European hornet: Species of wasp. The European hornet (Vespa crabro) is the largest eusocial wasp native to Europe.
Historically used in the 18th century to track down escaped slaves, this large Brazilian dog breed of mastiff type now also serves as a guard dog and companion — which breed?
Fila Brasileiro: Brazilian breed of dog. The Fila Brasileiro (Portuguese pronunciation: [ˈfilɐ bɾaziˈlejɾu]) is a Brazilian breed of large working dog of mastiff type.
Also called the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon or Red Car Theory, this cognitive bias makes you notice something everywhere right after you first learn about it — what is it?
Frequency illusion: Kind of cognitive bias. The name "Baader–Meinhof phenomenon" was coined in 1994 by Terry Mullen in a letter to the St.

Germany's first professor of experimental physics is remembered both for the tree-like electrical discharge patterns named after him and for the witty posthumous notebooks he called "waste books" — who was he?
Georg Christoph Lichtenberg: German scientist and satirist (1742–1799)
Credited alongside Isaac Newton with inventing calculus, this German polymath also pioneered binary arithmetic and earned the nickname 'the last universal genius' — who is he?
This protein filament that grows from follicles in the skin is one of the defining traits of mammals, and its removal or styling carries different meanings across cultures — what is it?
Hair: Protein filament that grows from follicles found in the dermis, or skin.
Nicknamed for its shaggy white spines that dangle over a centimeter long, this edible mushroom is commonly called lion's mane and is used in traditional Chinese medicine — which fungus?
Hericium erinaceus: Edible mushroom. Hericium erinaceus, commonly known as lion's mane, yamabushitake, bearded tooth fungus, or bearded hedgehog, is a species of tooth fungus.
This climbing, hemp-family plant's female cone-shaped flowers are used to flavor and preserve beer — what's the scientific name for hops?
Humulus lupulus: Species of flowering plant.
Named from an Ancient Greek word for 'intestinal obstruction,' this medical condition disrupts the gut's normal propulsive movement, whether from lost peristalsis or a physical blockage — what is it?
Ileus: Disruption to the propulsive ability of the intestine.
A self-taught rocketeer and practicing occultist, this co-founder of both JPL and Aerojet invented the first castable composite rocket propellant before dying young in 1952. Who was he?
Court astronomer and advisor to Elizabeth I, this mathematician-occultist kept one of England's largest libraries and is credited with coining the term "British Empire" — who was he?
John Dee: English scientist and occultist (1527–1608/09)
Convicted in 1995 of fraud and illegally intercepting communications, this hacker served five years in prison before founding his own computer-security consulting firm — who is he?
Known to some as Al-Kashi's theorem, this trigonometric rule relates a triangle's three side lengths to the cosine of one of its angles — what is it called?
Law of cosines: Generalization of Pythagorean theorem.
Sold under the brand name Vyvanse, this prodrug of dextroamphetamine treats ADHD and moderate-to-severe binge eating disorder, taking effect within about 90 minutes — which medication?
Lisdexamfetamine: Central nervous system stimulant prodrug.
Painlessly swollen lymph nodes, drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss point to this family of white-blood-cell cancers, split mainly into Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin types — what is it?
Lymphoma: Hematologic cancer that affects lymphocytes.
The second woman ever to win the Nobel Prize in Physics (after Marie Curie) shared the 1963 award for her discoveries about nuclear shell structure — who was she?

Encompassing conditions marked by a clinically significant disturbance in thinking, emotional regulation, or behavior that causes real distress or impaired functioning, this broad psychiatric category has causes that remain often unclear — what is the umbrella term for it?
Based on a Soviet fighter jet but optimized for ground attack, this variable-sweep aircraft was license-built in India as the 'Bahadur,' or 'Valiant' — which jet?
Mikoyan MiG-27: Series of 1970s Soviet attack aircraft.

First identified from skulls found in a Dutch chalk quarry near Maastricht and initially mistaken for crocodile or whale bones, this giant marine lizard genus lived until 66 million years ago — which genus is it?
Mosasaurus: Extinct genus of marine lizard from the Late Cretaceous.
Colloquially known as a moon, this type of astronomical body orbits a planet or dwarf planet, with 455 confirmed examples across the Solar System's six major systems — what is it called?
Natural satellite: Astronomical body that orbits a planet. Natural satellites are colloquially referred to as moons, by analogy with the Moon, Earth's natural satellite.
Made from red algae and dried into flat sheets through a process resembling papermaking, this ingredient has wrapped sushi and rice balls in Japan since the 700s — what is it?
Nori: Edible seaweed species of the red algae genus Pyropia.
Its Greek name means 'serpent-bearer,' and it's depicted as a man grasping a snake represented by a neighboring constellation — which constellation straddles the celestial equator?
Ophiuchus: Constellation straddling the celestial equator. Ophiuchus ( o-fee-YOO-kəs) is a large constellation straddling the celestial equator.
This butterfly was the first species to be given the common name now applied to its entire family, and is widespread across the Palearctic and North America — which species?
Papilio machaon: Species of insect. Papilio machaon, the Old World swallowtail, is a butterfly of the family Papilionidae.
By learning to synthesize hormones from plant sterols — even wild Mexican yams — this research chemist laid the foundation for cortisone and the birth-control pill. Who was this pioneer?
Percy Lavon Julian: American research chemist (1899–1975)

For two thousand years it lived inside natural philosophy alongside chemistry and biology, only breaking off as its own discipline during the 17th-century Scientific Revolution; what is this study of matter, energy, and force?
Physics: Scientific field of study. It is one of the most fundamental scientific disciplines.
First domesticated some 5,000 years ago on the Iranian plateau, this fruit-bearing shrub reached California in 1769 via Spanish settlers — which fruit?
Pomegranate: Fruit-bearing deciduous shrub. Pomegranate was first domesticated by ancient Iranians in the Iranian plateau and nearby regions about 5,000 years ago.
This thorny European shrub's tart fruit gives sloe gin its name in Britain, while its wood becomes the classic Irish walking stick — what is it?
Prunus spinosa: Species of flowering plant in the rose family.
Domesticated in Asia, this crunchy root vegetable in the mustard family owes its peppery bite to compounds like glucosinolate — what vegetable is it?
Radish: Root vegetable of the Brassicaceae family. The radish (Raphanus sativus or Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. sativus) is a flowering plant in the mustard family, Brassicaceae.

Grown for its fleshy, edible stalks since before the 18th century in Europe and Scandinavia, this plant's broad triangular leaves are actually poisonous due to their high oxalic acid content. What is it?
Rhubarb: Species of herbaceous perennial plant with fleshy, sour edible stalks.
First identified in November 2002 and traced through civets to horseshoe bats in Yunnan, this viral respiratory disease had an 11% fatality rate before its outbreak ended in 2003 — which disease?
Creator of a satirical comic strip about corporate cubicle life, this cartoonist also wrote the pandeistic novella 'God's Debris' — who is he?
Scott Adams: American cartoonist and author (1957–2026)
This crustacean typically swims forward using its swimmerets but can flick its tail to dart backward in a defensive move called 'lobstering' — what is it?
